What has to match

Puzzle 27's Run Script works on your Mac. Then the build server, a Linux machine, can't make the framework; an iOS colleague updates Xcode and the Kotlin build breaks; and the app wants to run on an older iPhone than your framework. Here are the three things that must match, and where each is written down.

  • Puzzle 27: How Xcode builds your Kotlin

    Xcode builds an app as an ordered list of build phases. A Run Script phase placed before Compile Sources runs ./gradlew :shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode, which links the one framework for the platform and configuration Xcode is building, then copies it into Xcode's own build output and signs it. So Swift finds the framework without any path set by hand, and a dynamic framework is embedded for you.

    Review puzzle 27

The problem

Puzzle 27's Run Script builds your framework on your Mac, every time Xcode builds. Then three things go wrong in one month. The team's build server, a Linux machine, runs the release task from puzzle 26 and fails. An iOS colleague installs the newest Xcode, and the Kotlin build starts failing on their Mac only. And the product team wants the app to keep running on iPhones with an older iOS than your framework was built for. None of this is about your Kotlin code. What has to match?

See it

The building block

The first thing is the machine that runs the build, the build host. Kotlin's docs list which hosts can build what, and for Apple targets the split is exactly puzzle 23's two stages:

Build hostFinal binaries (the link stage)klibs (the compile stage)
a Mac, Apple chip or Intelany supported targetany supported target
Linux or Windowsany target except Apple'sApple targets too, with one exception not taught yet

The docs say it plainly: "Building final binaries for Apple targets on Linux and Windows is also not possible." So a build server can check and compile your shared code for iOS on Linux, but the job that links the framework or the XCFramework, and every iOS test run, needs a Mac.

The second thing is Xcode's version. Kotlin's docs say that "to compile Apple targets, you need to install Xcode and its command-line tools": the Kotlin build itself uses tools that come with Xcode. So each Kotlin version is tested with one Xcode version. Kotlin's compatibility guide keeps the table; two rows of it:

KotlinXcode it's tested with
2.4.20–2.4.2126.4
2.3.20–2.3.2126.0

So when the iOS team moves to a new Xcode, check the table and move Kotlin with it; and when you upgrade Kotlin, check which Xcode it expects. Kotlin even removes targets to keep up: it deprecated one 32-bit watch target "to ensure compatibility with Xcode 27".

The third thing is the oldest iOS version. An iOS app has a deployment target: in Apple's words, "your app's minimum deployment target defines the range of operating system versions your app supports". Your Kotlin framework has a minimum of its own: by default, Kotlin builds Apple targets for iOS 15.0 and later. The app can't promise to run where its framework wasn't built to run, so keep the app's deployment target at 15.0 or higher. If the app really must support an older iOS, lower Kotlin's minimum on purpose, with a line Kotlin's docs give:

freeCompilerArgs += "-Xoverride-konan-properties=minVersion.ios=14.0"

The analogy

The print shop from puzzle 23 only owns the presses for Apple's paper in one city, so the final print run happens there, though manuscripts can be typeset anywhere. Its presses are certified for one model of stitching machine at a time: when the restaurant's supplier changes the model, the shop upgrades too. And a cookbook printed for kitchens built after 2021 can't be promised to a restaurant whose oldest kitchen is from 2020, unless the shop prints a special edition.

Check yourself

Your build server runs Linux. Which of these can it still do for your iOS targets?

Right. Linux: klibs yes, Apple binaries no.

Not quite. It runs on Linux, and can produce klibs for Apple targets; only the link stage for them needs a Mac.

Not quite. Final binaries for Apple targets can be built only on a Mac.

An iOS colleague installs a newer Xcode than your Kotlin version is listed with, and the Kotlin build fails on their Mac only. Why does Xcode's version matter to a Kotlin build at all?

Right. Kotlin and Xcode versions move together.

Not quite. Xcode never compiles Kotlin: Kotlin/Native does, then links with Xcode's tools.

Not quite. The Kotlin build itself uses Xcode's tools, so a version it wasn't tested with can break it. Re-read that part ↑

The app's deployment target is iOS 14.0, and your Kotlin framework uses Kotlin's default minimum. What's the problem, and one fix?

Not quite. The framework was built for 15.0 and later, so it's not promised to work on 14.

Right. The app can't support older iOS than its framework.

Not quite. Static or dynamic doesn't change which iOS versions the code was built for. Re-read that part ↑

What you now know

Kotlin/Native builds final binaries for Apple targets only on a Mac; Linux and Windows can still produce klibs. Each Kotlin version is tested with one Xcode version, listed in Kotlin's compatibility table, so upgrade the two together. And a Kotlin framework supports iOS 15.0 and later by default, so the app's deployment target must be at least that, or you lower Kotlin's minimum on purpose.
